title: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom.
description:
Old church windows are thicker at the bottom. The story goes that over 800 years the glass crept downward under its own weight. It is the most repeated fact about glass, and it is false.

You would wait out the universe, and then some. Physicists estimate the flow would take around a hundred thousand billion billion years. The universe is under fourteen billion years old. Medieval glass has not had a rounding error of the time it would need.

They were made that way, then stood that way up. Medieval glass was blown into cylinders, split and flattened by hand, so no sheet came out even. Glaziers simply set the thick edge at the bottom. The 'flow' is a fitter's choice, held for 800 years.

Glass is not quite a solid either. It is its own state, on a clock nobody will ever read out.

Sources:
- https://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/glass-transition/myth.php (University of Cambridge DoITPoMS, 'Do Cathedral Glasses Flow?'; read in full 26 Aug 2026): establishes the myth that over centuries cathedral window glass flows downward under gravity, leaving panes thicker at the bottom; that Zanotto and Gupta calculated the room-temperature relaxation time for such flow at about ten to the power of 23 years, far beyond the age of the Universe at about ten to the power of 10 years; and the real cause, that medieval glass was blown into large cylinders which were split and flattened by hand so it was never of even thickness, with fitters instinctively placing the thicker edge at the bottom. Cites E.D. Zanotto, 'Do cathedral glasses flow?', American Journal of Physics 66, 392-395 (1998).
- https://www.livescience.com/chemistry/is-glass-a-liquid-or-a-solid (Live Science, Victoria Atkinson, 24 Sep 2023; read in full 26 Aug 2026): materials scientist John Mauro of Penn State says glass is neither a true liquid nor a true solid but its own distinct, nonequilibrium, noncrystalline state that appears solid on short timescales and relaxes towards a liquid only over billions of years; John Parker of the Sheffield Centre for Glass Research says that in a practical sense glass is a rigid solid on any sensible timescale, and that the old panes are thicker at the bottom because a thousand years ago makers could not produce glass of uniform thickness.
